subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. Pankaj came down in his new shirt for the school photo. His elder brother Suraj looked up from his toast. "That colour makes you look ill." Pankaj changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.
Wednesday. Pankaj showed Suraj his science model. "The wiring's messy. It'll short." Pankaj snatched it back and slammed his door.
Friday. The model had shorted in class, just as Suraj said. That evening Pankaj knocked on his brother's door. "You were right about the wiring. But when you say things like that, it sounds like you think I'm useless." Suraj stared. "I didn't mean it that way." "I know. Can you just tell me what's wrong and how to fix it, and skip the 'ill' part?" Suraj nodded slowly, then pulled out a screwdriver.

qa.q: What did Suraj say about Pankaj's shirt colour?
qa.a: "That colour makes you look ill."

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel after the shirt comment, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt hurt and criticised; he changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.

qa.q: What choice did Pankaj make on Friday, and what came of it?
qa.a: He told Suraj how the words landed and asked for the fix without the harsh part; Suraj nodded and got a screwdriver.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Pankaj said his words sound like "you think I'm useless"?
qa.a: He seems surprised, since he meant no harm, and may realise his honesty was landing as an attack.

grounding: A teenager hurt by his brother's blunt remarks tells him how the words land and asks for the honest content without the harsh tone.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage: Francis, come and sit by your Aparna aunty. You're sulking because your sister called your haircut a disaster? Let me tell you about my sister Leela. When I was fourteen, she told me my singing was flat, my handwriting looked like ants, and my best friend was using me. Every one of those stung. For a year I thought she hated me. Then one day, after she said my essay was "boring in the middle", I told her, "Leela, when you say it like that, I hear that I'm boring." She was shocked. She said she only meant the middle paragraph. We made a rule: she says the true part, I ask for the useful part. The essay won a prize. And my friend was using me, by the way. So, what exactly did she say about the haircut?

qa.q: What did Leela say Aparna's handwriting looked like?
qa.a: She said it looked like ants.

qa.q: What did young Aparna believe about Leela for a year, and why?
qa.a: She thought Leela hated her, because every blunt remark stung.

qa.q: What turning point changed how the sisters spoke to each other?
qa.a: Aparna told Leela how "boring in the middle" landed, and they made a rule: Leela says the true part, Aparna asks for the useful part.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt hearing Aparna say "I hear that I'm boring"?
qa.a: She was shocked, since she only meant one paragraph, and may have realised her honesty was landing as an insult.

grounding: An aunt recalls being stung by a blunt older sister, telling her how the words landed, and learning to keep the honest part and drop the sting.

passage:
First week of term. Harsha from Rukmini's lab group said he'd lost his wallet and needed five hundred rupees for the lab manual. Rukmini handed it over without a second thought.
Two weeks later. He asked again, for bus fare home, and whether she could "just type up" his lab report because he was swamped. She did both, staying up past midnight.
The following Saturday. In the canteen she heard him tell someone he'd been to three films that week. Something in her chest went tight. On Monday she found him. "I'm happy to study with you. But I can't lend more until the first two are back, and your report is yours to write." Harsha looked annoyed, then shrugged. She walked away shaky, but lighter.

qa.q: What did Harsha say he needed five hundred rupees for?
qa.a: He said he needed it for the lab manual.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she heard about the three films?
qa.a: Her chest went tight; she felt hurt and began to suspect her kindness was being used.

qa.q: What limit did Rukmini set on Monday, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: She offered to study together but refused more loans until the first two were back and handed the report back to him, keeping her generosity without being used.

qa.q: What might Harsha's annoyed look show about how he saw Rukmini's help?
qa.a: It suggests he had come to expect her help as a given, so a limit surprised him.

grounding: Over a few weeks a trusting young woman lends and helps freely, notices she is being used, and sets a limit.

passage:
Disha, you remind me of me at twenty. Your Mama trusted everyone. In college, a friend named Anil needed help every week: my notes, my scooter, a little money "till Friday". Friday never came, but I kept saying yes, because saying no felt mean. Then one night he borrowed the scooter and returned it with an empty tank and a dent, and not a word. I sat on the steps and felt like a fool. My father said something I still use: "Kindness is yours to give, not theirs to take." After that I asked myself one question: does this person give anything back, even a thank you? I still help people, Disha. I just stopped handing my keys to everyone who asks.
Your Divyansh Mama

qa.q: What condition was the scooter in when Anil returned it?
qa.a: It came back with an empty tank and a dent.

qa.q: What did young Divyansh feel sitting on the steps that night?
qa.a: He felt like a fool, realising his trust had been used.

qa.q: What question did Divyansh start asking himself after that night?
qa.a: Whether the person gives anything back, even a thank you, which let him keep helping without being used.

qa.q: What might Divyansh's father have wanted him to understand with 'Kindness is yours to give, not theirs to take'?
qa.a: His father probably wanted him to see that kindness is a choice, not a debt others can collect, so he could keep helping without being used.

grounding: An uncle recalls how his trusting generosity was used at twenty and how he learned to spot it and set limits.

passage:
Tuesday. Vidya caught Shankar outside the library. "Cover my café shift on Saturday? And help with my presentation slides? And come to my cousin's party?" Shankar thought for a second. "The slides, yes, I'm good at those. The shift, no. The party, no, I've got my own deadline." He didn't add a list of excuses.
Wednesday. Vidya was cool with him at lunch. Shankar felt his stomach twist, and let it. Her disappointment was real, but it wasn't a disaster.
Saturday. They sat together in the library, fixing her slides. "I was annoyed," Vidya admitted. "But you actually showed up for the thing you said yes to." Shankar smiled. "That's the idea."

qa.q: Which of Vidya's three requests did Shankar agree to?
qa.a: The slides.

qa.q: What did Shankar feel on Wednesday when Vidya was cool with him?
qa.a: His stomach twisted; he felt uneasy, but he let her disappointment be without rushing to undo his no.

qa.q: What choice did Shankar make on Tuesday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He said yes where it was true for him and a short no to the rest, then showed up fully for the slides.

qa.q: How did Vidya's view of Shankar's no change by Saturday?
qa.a: She was annoyed at first, but came to value that he reliably did what he agreed to.

grounding: A young man agrees where he truly can and declines the rest without long apologies, accepting Vidya's brief disappointment.

passage: Sit down, Sachin. You look like you've said yes to six things again. When I was your age, in my first job at the branch office, I apologised for every no. "So sorry, I really wish I could, it's just that..." Three minutes of it. People heard the apology and pushed, and I usually gave in. The manager then, an old man named Mr Dsouza, watched me do it once and said, "Uma, you're asking permission to refuse." So I practised. When a colleague asked me to take his Saturday audit, I said, "I can help you plan it on Friday. I can't do Saturday." Full stop. He grumbled for a day. By Monday he was fine, and I'd had my Saturday. A little disappointment isn't cruelty, Sachin. It's just honest.

qa.q: What did Mr Dsouza say Uma was doing when refusing?
qa.a: "You're asking permission to refuse."

qa.q: Why did young Uma apologise for every no?
qa.a: Uma seems to have felt uncomfortable disappointing people, as if a refusal needed a long excuse to be allowed.

qa.q: How did Uma change the way of refusing the Saturday audit?
qa.a: Uma offered help planning on Friday and said a plain no to Saturday, with no long apology.

qa.q: How did the colleague react to Uma's plain no, and what does that show?
qa.a: He grumbled for a day and was fine by Monday, showing that a little disappointment passes and is not cruelty.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls learning to decline plainly and warmly without a long apology, and that brief disappointment is not cruelty.

passage: Avni, I've watched you say "no problem" to everyone this month, and it reminds me of someone. Thirty years ago at this press, we had a proofreader called Mohan. Whoever was late, Mohan stayed back. Whoever fought, Mohan made tea and calmed them down. We all liked him, and none of us noticed that he hadn't had a raise in four years. When a new manager, Mrs Kurian, arrived, she read the night logs and saw his name on every late shift. At the next meeting she thanked him by name and split the late shifts on a rota. Mohan went red and said it was nothing. It wasn't. Things ran better once the load was shared. So, Avni, who is going to see your name in the logs?

qa.q: How long had Mohan gone without a raise?
qa.a: Mohan hadn't had a raise in four years.

qa.q: What does Mohan going red and calling it nothing suggest?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed by praise and unused to being noticed, though it clearly mattered.

qa.q: What choices did Mrs Kurian make after reading the night logs?
qa.a: She thanked Mohan by name and split the late shifts on a rota, sharing both the load and the credit.

qa.q: How might Mohan have felt about all those years of late shifts before Mrs Kurian noticed?
qa.a: He may have felt taken for granted, carrying the extra work quietly while nobody saw it.

grounding: A senior colleague remembers a helpful proofreader whose goodwill held the team together until a fair manager shared his load and recognition.

passage: The client demo was at four, the office generator had failed, and two of the team were stuck in a flooded underpass. Keerthana, leading the team for the first time, watched Alka do what she always did: find the spare laptop, calm the intern, rewrite the missing slides and fetch everyone water, without a word about herself. The demo went well. The client thanked Keerthana. Keerthana opened her mouth to say thank you, then noticed Alka already packing up to finish someone else's report. She checked the tracker: Alka's name was on nine tasks, most not her own. On the evening call she said, "The demo happened because of Alka," and moved four of those tasks to others. Alka blinked, surprised, then smiled.

qa.q: How many tasks was Alka's name on in the tracker?
qa.a: Alka's name was on nine tasks, most not her own.

qa.q: What does Alka's surprised blink on the evening call suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she is not used to being credited, and the recognition caught her off guard.

qa.q: What choices did Keerthana make after checking the tracker?
qa.a: She gave Alka credit on the call and moved four of her tasks to others, sharing both recognition and load.

qa.q: What might have happened to Alka if Keerthana had simply accepted the client's thanks?
qa.a: Alka's work would have stayed invisible and her load would have kept growing, risking burnout.

grounding: On a chaotic demo day a new team lead notices a supportive colleague is overloaded and unthanked, and shares the load and the credit.

passage: A leaf blower roars outside the Stockholm flat and Anders, twenty months old, bursts into sobs, arms stiff, face red. His father, Rafael, picks him up and holds him close, swaying. "Loud, loud. I've got you." Anders keeps crying for a long time, far longer than his cousin would. A neighbour in the stairwell frowns. Rafael keeps swaying and humming the same low tune. Slowly the sobs turn to hiccups, and Anders rests his cheek on Rafael's shoulder.

qa.q: What does Rafael say while swaying Anders?
qa.a: "Loud, loud. I've got you."

qa.q: What do Anders's stiff arms and red face suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He is frightened and overwhelmed by the sudden roar.

qa.q: What choice did Rafael make even when the neighbour frowned?
qa.a: He kept swaying and humming the same low tune, offering steady comfort until Anders settled.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel when the neighbour frowns?
qa.a: He may feel judged, as if the crying means bad parenting, but he stays calm and focused on Anders.

grounding: A sensitive toddler cries hard at a loud noise and takes a long time to settle, and his father's steady comfort helps.

passage: I'm Keerthana, a crèche helper. Every morning Uday, two, clings to his mother's dupatta and cries till he's hoarse. When nap time moved, he cried after lunch too; I can't be sure why. His mother once asked me, eyes wet, if she was doing something wrong. I told her no. We keep his blue blanket by the door, sing the same song each morning, and I hold him till he's ready. Last week he pointed at the fish tank sooner.

qa.q: What is kept by the door for Uday?
qa.a: His blue blanket is kept by the door.

qa.q: What might Uday's mother have been feeling when she asked if she was doing something wrong?
qa.a: She seemed worried and guilty, fearing the crying was her fault.

qa.q: What changes did the crèche make to help Uday settle?
qa.a: They kept his blue blanket by the door, sang the same song each morning and held him until he was ready.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Uday's crying?
qa.a: Keerthana treats it as his sensitivity, not bad behaviour or bad parenting, and answers it with steady comfort.

grounding: A crèche helper describes a toddler who cries hard at separation and changed routines, and reassures his mother it is not her fault.

passage: "What if the storm breaks the window? What if the thunder comes inside? What if you don't wake up?" Five-year-old Hiroshi asks in their Osaka flat, clutching his quilt. His mother, Dalia, doesn't say, "Don't be silly." She sits on the bed. "The window is strong glass. Thunder is only a sound. I'll be in the next room, and I'll check on you when I go to bed, like always." Then she does the same three things as every night: water glass, night-light, one song. Hiroshi asks one more what-if, quieter. By the second verse, his grip loosens.

qa.q: What three things does Dalia do every night?
qa.a: Water glass, night-light, one song.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi clutching his quilt suggest he feels?
qa.a: He is frightened; the storm worries feel real and big to him.

qa.q: What choice did Dalia make instead of telling Hiroshi not to be silly?
qa.a: She gave calm, simple answers and kept the same bedtime steps, which soothed him.

qa.q: What would change if Dalia had said there was nothing to fear and left?
qa.a: Hiroshi would likely feel his worry was not heard and lie awake more frightened.

grounding: A young child asks what-if questions about a storm at bedtime, and his mother's calm answers and familiar routine soothe him.

passage: At nap time in the daycare, Anjali, five, lies stiff on her mat with her eyes open. "What if Mumma is late today? What if the bus breaks? What if she forgets me?" Urmila, the carer, kneels beside her. "Mumma comes at five. When the big hand is on the twelve, the gate bell rings. If she's ever late, I stay with you until she comes. Every time." Anjali asks the same questions again, and Urmila answers them the same way, calmly. Then Urmila pats the mat three times, their nap signal. Anjali's eyes close. At five, the bell rings.

qa.q: What is Urmila and Anjali's nap signal?
qa.a: Urmila pats the mat three times.

qa.q: What is Anjali worried about as she lies stiff on her mat?
qa.a: She fears her Mumma will be late or forget her.

qa.q: What did Urmila do when Anjali asked the same questions again?
qa.a: Urmila answered them the same way, calmly, and gave the usual nap signal, which helped Anjali rest.

qa.q: How might Anjali's Mumma feel on hearing how Urmila handled the worry?
qa.a: She may feel grateful that her daughter was comforted rather than hushed.

grounding: A worried child asks what-if questions about her mother being late, and a carer's calm, repeated answers and routine soothe her.

passage: On spelling-test mornings in Bergen, Ingrid's stomach hurts before she has finished her porridge. Last Tuesday she also called her teacher "Mamma" by mistake, and the class giggled. She was still replaying it on Friday, lying in bed, her face hot all over again. Her dad, Siddiq, sat on the edge of the bed. "What's the feeling called, if you had to name it?" "Embarrassed. And scared for Monday's test." "Both at once. That's a lot." They made a small plan: she would practise five words each evening, and on Monday morning she'd tell him the tummy feeling out loud instead of hiding it. "And if the tummy aches keep happening, we'll ask the doctor too," he added.

qa.q: What did Ingrid call her teacher by mistake?
qa.a: She called her teacher "Mamma" by mistake.

qa.q: What two feelings does Ingrid name to her dad?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed about the slip and scared about Monday's test.

qa.q: What small plan did Ingrid and Siddiq make?
qa.a: She would practise five words each evening and say the tummy feeling out loud on Monday, and they would ask the doctor if the aches keep happening.

qa.q: How might the classmates who giggled remember the "Mamma" slip?
qa.a: They probably forgot it quickly, even though Ingrid replayed it for days.

grounding: A girl gets stomach aches before tests and replays a small embarrassment for days, and her father helps her name feelings and plan small steps.

passage: Ten minutes before the maths exam, Chinmay was in the school sick room again, curled on the bed, holding his stomach. The counsellor, Joseph, came in and pulled up a stool. "Is this the same feeling as before the science test?" Chinmay nodded. "And the thing at assembly?" Chinmay winced. Three weeks ago he had tripped on the stage steps, and he still went red thinking of it. Joseph handed him a card with faces drawn on it. "Point to the loudest one. Scared? Embarrassed?" Chinmay pointed to both. "Okay. One small step: sit the first section only, then come and tell me how it went. And if these stomach aches keep coming, we'll talk to your parents about the doctor." Chinmay stood up slowly. He finished the whole paper.

qa.q: What did Chinmay trip on three weeks ago?
qa.a: He tripped on the stage steps.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay wince when the assembly was mentioned?
qa.a: He was still embarrassed, replaying the trip weeks later.

qa.q: What small step did Joseph suggest, and how did it turn out?
qa.a: Joseph suggested sitting only the first section and reporting back; Chinmay finished the whole paper.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's classmates see his visits to the sick room?
qa.a: They may not realise how strongly he feels things, and could think he is just avoiding exams.

grounding: A boy gets stomach aches before exams and replays an embarrassment for weeks, and a counsellor helps him name feelings and take one small step.

passage:
Monday. Rajni got 14 out of 25 in chemistry and snapped at her little sister for humming. By evening she was sure her friends thought she was stupid.
Wednesday. A pimple on her chin. She wore her hair over her face all day and skipped the lunch table. Her friend Sonali texted, "u ok?" Rajni typed "fine" and then cried in the bathroom, not even sure why.
Saturday. She laughed through a whole film with Sonali, then felt low again at bedtime. Her mother found her awake and sat down. "Up and down this week?" Rajni nodded. "That's very common at fifteen. We'll keep an eye on it together. If it ever starts stopping you from school or friends, we'll talk to someone who helps with this." Rajni leaned on her shoulder.

qa.q: What did Rajni score in chemistry?
qa.a: Rajni got 14 out of 25 in chemistry.

qa.q: What did Rajni believe about her friends on Monday evening?
qa.a: She was sure her friends thought she was stupid, a doubt that grew out of one test mark.

qa.q: What did Rajni's mother do on Saturday night that helped?
qa.a: She named the ups and downs calmly, said they are common, and agreed to watch them together and get help if they ever stop daily life.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt when Rajni texted "fine" and skipped lunch?
qa.a: Sonali may have felt worried and unsure, sensing something was wrong but not being let in.

grounding: Over a week a teenager swings between irritation, worry and low confidence about marks, looks and friends, and her mother treats it as common while watching for more.

passage: Rukmini, you think you're the only one who wants to hide under a blanket one hour and throw a pillow the next? At fourteen I once cried because my plait was uneven, and an hour later I shouted at my father for asking about homework. I hated my voice, my nose, my maths marks, sometimes all at once. Your Chandrika Masi was a storm. My Amma would wait until it passed, and then she would bring tea and ask, "Big storm or small storm today?" Most were small. One winter they weren't; I stopped wanting to go to school at all, and Amma took me to talk to a counsellor. That helped a lot. So, beta, is today a big storm or a small one?

qa.q: What made Chandrika cry at fourteen?
qa.a: Her plait was uneven.

qa.q: How did young Chandrika feel about herself at fourteen?
qa.a: She was full of self-doubt, hating her voice, her nose and her maths marks, sometimes all at once.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's Amma do when the storms got too big one winter?
qa.a: When Chandrika stopped wanting to go to school at all, Amma took her to talk to a counsellor, which helped.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's Amma have felt, waiting for each storm to pass?
qa.a: Amma was probably patient but watchful, trusting most storms would pass while staying close enough to see when one winter was bigger.

grounding: An aunt tells Rukmini about her own teenage mood swings and self-doubt, and how help came when it stopped daily life.

passage:
Dear Anjali,
I'm writing this on paper because I know you read messages ten times looking for hidden meaning, and I wanted you to have something you can hold. You cancelled the planetarium again on Saturday, twenty minutes before. I won't pretend I wasn't disappointed. But I'm not angry, and I don't think you're being dramatic. I've seen your hands shake before you walk into a crowded place. So here's my plan: I'll keep inviting you. Every time. If you can come, great. If you can't, I'll send you a photo of whatever we saw. And no one-letter replies from me, I promise; I'll write full sentences.
Your friend,
Varun

qa.q: How long before the planetarium trip did Anjali cancel?
qa.a: Twenty minutes before.

qa.q: What does Varun believe about why Anjali cancels?
qa.a: Varun doesn't think Anjali is being dramatic, having seen Anjali's hands shake before crowded places.

qa.q: What choice does Varun make about future plans?
qa.a: Varun decides to keep inviting Anjali every time and to send photos when Anjali can't come, staying steady and consistent.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel on reading that the invitations will keep coming?
qa.a: Anjali may feel less alone and less guilty, knowing that cancelling won't end the friendship.

grounding: A friend writes to Anjali, who overthinks messages and cancels at the last minute, promising patient, steady invitations.

passage: You asked why I keep my phone on loud at night, Didi. It's Pema. If I reply "ok" instead of "okay!!", she spends an hour wondering if I'm angry with her. She's told me so: "Disha, I thought you were angry." She cancels outings at the last minute, and at first I thought she was just flaking. Then one day at the bus stop I saw her face go white when a big group got on, and she stepped back and let the bus go. That's not drama. So I changed a few things. I send voice notes, so she can hear I'm fine. I tell her plans early, with who's coming. And when she cancels, I just say, "No worries, next time," and I mean it. Last week she came to the whole birthday party.

qa.q: What did Pema do at the bus stop when a big group got on?
qa.a: Her face went white, and she stepped back and let the bus go.

qa.q: What worries Pema when a reply is short?
qa.a: She worries Disha is angry with her and spends an hour wondering about it.

qa.q: What changes did Disha make after the bus stop moment?
qa.a: Disha sent voice notes, shared plans early with who was coming, and answered cancellations with a calm "next time".

qa.q: How might Pema have felt going to the whole birthday party?
qa.a: She may have felt safer because Disha had been steady and patient, so the party felt less frightening.

grounding: A teenager describes Pema, who overthinks messages and cancels plans, and how patience and consistency help her feel less alone.

passage: Akash, sit with your Jasleen Bua. Your heart is racing before the board exam, and you think it means something terrible will happen. At your age I thought the same. The night before my Class 10 exams my chest thumped and I was sure I'd fail. My Biji didn't say "relax". She said, "The drum is telling you to slow down, not that the sky is falling." We walked twice round the gurdwara compound, I told her every worry out loud, and then I slept. Later, in college, when the worry stopped me sleeping for weeks, Biji was the one who said, "Now we see a doctor who knows about minds." That helped too. So, puttar, walk with me, tell me the worries, and then bed.

qa.q: What did Biji say the drum was telling young Jasleen?
qa.a: To slow down, not that the sky is falling.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to feel about his racing heart before the exam?
qa.a: He seems frightened, thinking the racing heart means something terrible will happen in the exam.

qa.q: What steps did Biji use the night before Jasleen's exams?
qa.a: They walked twice round the compound, Jasleen said every worry aloud, and then slept.

qa.q: How might Biji have seen young Jasleen's thumping chest that night?
qa.a: Biji seems to have seen it as a signal to slow down, not a disaster, and trusted that walking and talking would settle the worry.

grounding: An aunt shows her nephew how to read big feelings as signals to slow down, using movement, naming worries, sleep and, when it persists, a professional.

passage: The bus to the state quiz final broke down on the highway, and Abhinav's team arrived with eight minutes to spare, into a hall packed with noise. His heart started hammering. The old thought came: something is wrong. Then the newer one: this is a signal to slow down, not proof. He walked once up and down the corridor, fast, shaking out his hands. "Vaibhav," he said to his teammate, "I'm nervous. Like, a lot." Vaibhav bumped his shoulder. "Same. Take the science round?" Abhinav nodded. Last term, when the worry had kept him awake for weeks, he had told his parents, and they had found a counsellor he still saw on Thursdays. Tonight he would sleep. Right now, he would answer.

qa.q: How many minutes to spare did the team have when they arrived?
qa.a: They arrived with eight minutes to spare.

qa.q: What was Abhinav thinking when his heart started hammering?
qa.a: First the old thought that something was wrong, then the newer one that it was a signal to slow down, not proof.

qa.q: Which steps did Abhinav take before the quiz, and why did they help?
qa.a: He walked the corridor shaking out his hands and told Vaibhav he was nervous, which steadied him enough to play.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have felt when Abhinav admitted being nervous?
qa.a: Vaibhav seems relieved to share it, answering "Same", and the honesty makes both feel less alone.

grounding: Under a stressful delay, a teenager treats his racing heart as a signal to slow down, moves, names his worry to a teammate, and keeps seeing a counsellor.
